claim: Small molecules up to 20–40 kDa (i.e., up to roughly 5 nm in diameter) can diffuse freely through the NPC.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The passage of larger macromolecules is impeded unless they are bound to nuclear transport receptors (NTRs).

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpc for NTF2 binding to Nsp1 is 0.34 ± 0.02 kBT.
evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpc for Importin β binding to Nsp1 is 0.40 ± 0.02 kBT.
evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpp for Nup98-glyco is 0.030 ± 0.002 kBT.
evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpc for NTF2 binding to Nup98-glyco is 0.36 ± 0.02 kBT.
evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpp for reg-FSFG is 0.030 ± 0.005 kBT.
evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpc for NTF2 binding to reg-FSFG is 0.40 ± 0.02 kBT.
evidence: This is a result from matching the computational model to experimental data, shown in Table 2.

claim: εpp for Nup98-glyco exceeded that of Nsp1.
source: From the comparison of computation and experiment, it was clear that εpp for Nup98-glyco exceeded that of Nsp1, in good agreement with our previous study (Eisele et al., 2013), in which we also found Nup98-glyco to be more cohesive than Nsp1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the εpp values determined from the computational model, and is consistent with prior work.

claim: Nup98-glyco is more cohesive than Nsp1.
source: in good agreement with our previous study (Eisele et al., 2013), in which we also found Nup98-glyco to be more cohesive than Nsp1.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Nup98-glyco and reg-FSFG have similar cohesiveness.
source: Nup98-glyco and reg-FSFG have similar cohesiveness.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the εpp values determined from the computational model.

claim: Using similar computational modeling in a NPC-mimicking pore geometry of 50 nm diameter, εpp ≈ 0.05 kBT was estimated from nanomechanical studies on intact NPCs.
source: Using similar computational modeling in a NPC-mimicking pore geometry of 50 nm diameter, we had previously estimated εpp ≈ 0.05 kBT from nanomechanical studies on intact NPCs (Bestembayeva et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The εpp value from nanomechanical studies on intact NPCs is close to the εpp values found in this study, though slightly higher.
source: This is close to the εpp values found here, though slightly higher, probably because the presence of NTRs was not taken into account in the computational model to which the nanomechanical data were matched.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and prior work, with a speculation about the reason for the difference.

claim: The precise setting of the NTR•FG domain interaction εpc strongly influenced the amount of bound NTRs for any given NTR concentration.
source: For a given cohesiveness parameter εpp, we found that the precise setting of the NTR•FG domain interaction εpc strongly influenced the amount of bound NTRs for any given NTR concentration, by orders of magnitude for 0.1 kBT changes in εpc, in the explored parameter range of 0.1 to 0.5 kBT.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2-5.

claim: The precise setting of εpc strongly affected the overall shape of the binding isotherms.
source: It also strongly affected the overall shape of the binding isotherms (Figure 3—figure supplements 2B, 3B, 4B and 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in the figure supplements.

claim: The agreement between computational data and experimental results is remarkably good.
source: Taking into account that these are fits with a single free parameter (εpc) over several orders of magnitude in bound NTR and in NTR concentration, the agreement with the experimental data is remarkably good.
evidence: This is an assessment of the quality of the fit between model and experiment shown in Figure 4.

claim: The estimates of εpc vary less than ~20% between the different FG domains and NTRs.
source: Table 2 summarizes the results of this analysis, with the estimates of εpc varying less than ~20% between the different FG domains and NTRs.
evidence: This is a summary of the results shown in Table 2.

claim: The measured binding of NTRs to FG domain films was accurately modeled by treating all amino acids in the FG domain chains identically and the NTR surfaces as homogeneous.
source: Taken together, the measured binding of NTRs to FG domain films was accurately modeled by our simplified description of the relevant interactions in terms of the two key parameters εpp and εpc, where we treat all amino acids in the FG domain chains identically and the NTR surfaces as homogeneous.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the computational modeling results.

claim: The results correspond to a few kBT binding energy per FG-binding site on the NTRs, in reasonable agreement with the millimolar affinities per FG motif observed with Importin β.
source: Hence our results would correspond to a few kBT binding energy per FG-binding site on the NTRs, in reasonable agreement with the millimolar affinities per FG motif observed with Impβ (Milles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison between the calculated binding energies and prior experimental measurements.

claim: Given parameter settings that best match the experimental system, the NTRs effectively penetrate and fill all FG domain films at cNTR = 10 μM.
source: They reveal that, given parameter settings that best match the experimental system (Table 2), the NTRs effectively penetrate and fill all FG domain films.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model shown in Figure 5 (top row).

claim: A relatively small change in the FG domain cohesiveness can have a dramatic effect on the NTR distribution.
source: Figure 5 (bottom row) demonstrates that a relatively small change in the FG domain cohesiveness can have a dramatic effect on the NTR distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5 (bottom row).

claim: With the NTF2•reg-FSFG interaction maintained at εpc = 0.4 kBT, an increase in inter-FG domain attraction by 33%, from εpp = 0.03 kBT to 0.04 kBT, essentially impaired NTF2 accumulation inside the film.
source: For example, with the NTF2•reg-FSFG interaction maintained at εpc = 0.4 kBT, an increase in inter-FG domain attraction by 33%, from εpp = 0.03 kBT to 0.04 kBT, essentially impaired NTF2 accumulation inside the film, and the NTF2 was enriched instead at the film-solution interface – that is to say, on the film rather than in the film.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5 (bottom row).

claim: A minor reduction in the colloid•FG domain interaction strength drastically reduces binding.
source: The model also indicated that a minor reduction in the colloid•FG domain interaction strength drastically reduces binding (Figure 3—figure supplements 2, 3 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in the figure supplements.

claim: By reducing εpc by only 25% compared to the best match for the respective NTRs and FG domains, there is a reduction in colloid binding by more than one order of magnitude at 1.4 μM colloid concentration.
source: Figure 6 illustrates this for a selected colloid concentration (1.4 μM, in the range of individual NTR concentrations in the cell) in the solution phase, and shows that by reducing εpc by only 25% compared to the best match for the respective NTRs and FG domains, there is a reduction in colloid binding by more than one order of magnitude.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 6.

claim: The native system is tuned to operate within a rather narrow parameter space in εpc and εpp that facilitates the strong enrichment of NTRs within the FG domain film.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the native system is tuned to operate within a rather narrow parameter space in εpc and εpp that facilitates the strong enrichment of NTRs within the FG domain film, whereas similarly sized proteins with weaker binding strength are effectively excluded.
evidence: This is an inference from the computational modeling results showing the sensitivity to parameter changes.

claim: Similarly sized proteins with weaker binding strength are effectively excluded from FG domain assemblies.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the native system is tuned to operate within a rather narrow parameter space in εpc and εpp that facilitates the strong enrichment of NTRs within the FG domain film, whereas similarly sized proteins with weaker binding strength are effectively excluded.
evidence: This is an inference from the computational modeling results showing the sensitivity to εpc.

claim: FG domain assemblies are significantly compacted compared to non-cohesive polymer brushes.
source: From the comparison between experimental and computational results for the thickness of the different FG domain films (in the absence of NTRs, Figure 3B), it appears that the FG domain assemblies are compacted by a factor two to four compared to a film of perfectly non-cohesive (εpp = 0, equivalent to a self-avoiding random walk model) and flexible peptide chains, as follows from an extrapolation of the computational data (dashed lines in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing experimental and computational results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The measured film thickness for Nsp1 is larger than the inner radius of the S. cerevisiae NPC (18 to 20 nm).
source: In spite of this condensation, the measured film thickness (Figure 1) for Nsp1 is larger than the inner radius of the S. cerevisiae NPC (18 to 20 nm [Alber et al., 2007; Yang et al., 1998])
evidence: This is a comparison between the experimental data and literature values for NPC dimensions.

claim: The measured film thickness for Nup98-glyco is more than 60% of the inner radius of the X. tropicalis NPC (~25 nm).
source: and that for Nup98-glyco more than 60% of the inner radius of the X. tropicalis NPC (~25 nm [Eibauer et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is a comparison between the experimental data and literature values for NPC dimensions.

claim: The results are consistent with the FG domains forming a pore-filling cohesive meshwork or condensed polymer brush.
source: This would be consistent with the FG domains forming a pore-filling cohesive meshwork or condensed polymer brush, as implied by the selective phase model (Frey and Gorlich, 2007; Frey et al., 2006; Hulsmann et al., 2012; Ribbeck and Gorlich, 2001), at least for Nsp1 in S. cerevisiae, and possibly for Nup98-glyco in X. tropicalis taking into account the nanopore confinement (Osmanovic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of prior models, supported by citations.

claim: Negative cooperativity appears robust against variations in NTR and in the spread of FG motifs between Nsp1, Nup98-glyco, and reg-FSFG.
source: Key findings of the present work are that this negative cooperativity appears robust against variations in NTR and in the spread of FG motifs between Nsp1, Nup98-glyco, and reg-FSFG
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings from the experimental data.

claim: Negative cooperativity can be reproduced, over orders of magnitude in NTR concentration, by a model that considers the FG domains as homogeneous polymers and the NTRs as featureless spheres.
source: and that it can be reproduced, over orders of magnitude in NTR concentration, by a model that considers the FG domains as homogeneous polymers and the NTRs as featureless spheres, i.e., ignoring chemical and structural heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings from the computational modeling.

claim: NTR binding is largely determined by generic effects such as overall binding energy, crowding and excluded-volume interactions, and by the entropic costs of NTR absorption.
source: Our analysis suggests that NTR binding is largely determined by generic effects such as overall binding energy, crowding and excluded-volume interactions, and by the entropic costs of NTR absorption that, in turn, reduce the conformational freedom of the grafted and flexible FG domains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results.

claim: At physiological NTR concentrations, the absorption of NTRs roughly doubles the total density of the films.
source: Such effects may well be expected since, at physiological NTR concentrations, the absorption of NTRs roughly doubles the total density of the films (Figure 5, top row).
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: Enrichment of NTRs in an FG domain phase vastly differs from NTR•FG motif binding under dilute conditions.
source: In this context, it is important to emphasize that enrichment of NTRs in an FG domain phase – in our model films but also in the NPC – vastly differs from NTR•FG motif binding under dilute conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of the NPC.

claim: The higher total Importin β•Nsp1 binding energy does not translate into a higher enrichment than for NTF2, even in the limit of low NTR concentrations.
source: This can be illustrated, for example, by comparing the enrichment of Nsp1 films for NTF2 and Impβ: the higher total Impβ•Nsp1 binding energy (integrated over the Impβ surface) does not translate into a higher enrichment than for NTF2, even in the limit of low NTR concentrations (Figures 1 and 4, top rows).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental and computational data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The binding energy is balanced by excluded-volume interactions and polymer cohesiveness and entropy.
source: The binding energy is balanced by excluded-volume interactions and polymer cohesiveness and entropy, i.e., by generic physical effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results.

claim: At equilibrium, the balance of interactions is such that NTRs can exchange between the NPC and the nucleus/cytoplasm at minimal cost.
source: At equilibrium, this balance is such that, in spite of the high binding energy between NTRs and FG domains, NTRs can exchange between the NPC and the nucleus/cytoplasm at minimal cost, thus facilitating cargo uptake and release.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of NPC function.

claim: A small reduction in εpc produces a dramatic decrease in the uptake of colloids by the FG domain films.
source: Remarkably, this overall balance appears rather finely tuned in several respects. Firstly, a small reduction in εpc produces a dramatic decrease in the uptake of colloids by the FG domain films (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 6.

claim: The strong dependence on εpc explains how FG domain assemblies in the NPC greatly favor the uptake of NTRs over other cytosolic proteins.
source: This is of major functional importance: by its strong dependence on εpc, the variable colloid uptake explains how FG domain assemblies in the NPC greatly favor the uptake of NTRs over other cytosolic proteins, which have been inferred to also bind FG domains (Hough et al., 2015), albeit more weakly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results in the context of NPC function, with support from a citation.

claim: Other cytosolic proteins have been inferred to also bind FG domains, albeit more weakly than NTRs.
source: which have been inferred to also bind FG domains (Hough et al., 2015), albeit more weakly.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Because of the selective uptake, NTRs can efficiently translocate across the NPC while more weakly binding proteins cannot.
source: This then explains how, because of the selective uptake, NTRs can efficiently translocate across the NPC while more weakly binding proteins cannot.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results in the context of NPC function.

claim: The NTRs appear to favor the penetration of and binding into the FG domain assemblies, but only just so.
source: In addition, from our comparison between experiment and computational modeling, the NTRs appear to favor the penetration of and binding into the FG domain assemblies, but only just so: penetration is inhibited for slightly larger FG domain cohesiveness (i.e., larger εpp), which results in NTRs preferentially binding on top of (and not into) the FG domain assembly (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: Penetration is inhibited for slightly larger FG domain cohesiveness, which results in NTRs preferentially binding on top of the FG domain assembly.
source: penetration is inhibited for slightly larger FG domain cohesiveness (i.e., larger εpp), which results in NTRs preferentially binding on top of (and not into) the FG domain assembly (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cohesiveness of the FG domains is tuned to be as tight as possible to optimize exclusion of inert proteins by their size, while still sufficiently loose to facilitate penetration by NTRs.
source: This is consistent with the remarkable selectivity exhibited by NPC transport and suggests that the cohesiveness of the FG domains is tuned to be as tight as possible to optimize exclusion of inert proteins by their size (Eisele et al., 2013), while still sufficiently loose to facilitate penetration by NTRs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results in the context of NPC function, with support from a citation.

claim: Large structural changes can occur within the determined parameter range of εpp in the pore geometry of the NPC.
source: Extrapolating our results on planar assemblies to the pore geometry of the NPC, we note that large structural changes can occur within the here determined parameter range of εpp: In analogous calculations for FG domains in an NPC-mimicking pore geometry of 50 nm diameter (Osmanovic et al., 2012; 2013b), we observed a transition (Osmanovic et al., 2012) between, on one hand, a central and pore-occluding condensate of FG domains in the NPC conduit, and on the other hand, a more open state with FG domains localized closer to the pore wall (see, e.g., Figure 7 in Osmanovic et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a reference to prior computational work by the authors in a different geometry.

claim: Such large and collective transitions are required to facilitate transport of larger cargo•NTR complexes through the NPC.
source: Such large and collective transitions are required to facilitate transport of larger cargo•NTR complexes, with a size comparable to the nuclear pore diameter, through the NPC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results in the context of NPC function.

claim: FG domain assemblies may adopt qualitatively different behaviors depending on the interaction strengths.
source: Depending on the interaction strengths, FG domains assemblies may thus adopt qualitatively different behaviors, e.g., absorption versus adsorption of NTRs and different types of polymer condensation.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the computational modeling.

claim: The overall FG domain interactions and NTR•FG affinity appear to be tuned close to the boundaries that separate different types of behaviors.
source: The overall FG domain interactions and NTR•FG affinity appear to be tuned close to the boundaries that separate these types of behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results showing sensitivity to parameter changes.

claim: The observed sensitivity to parameter values offers an explanation of why different modeling approaches have led to qualitatively different predictions of FG domain behavior in the NPC.
source: The observed sensitivity to the values assigned to parameters offers an explanation of why different modeling approaches thus far have led to qualitatively different predictions of FG domain behavior in the NPC (Ando et al., 2013; 2014; Gamini et al., 2014; Ghavami et al., 2014; Miao and Schulten, 2009; Mincer and Simon, 2011; Moussavi-Baygi et al., 2011a; 2011b; Opferman et al., 2012; 2013; Osmanovic et al., 2012; 2013b; Popken et al., 2015; Tagliazucchi et al., 2013; Wolf and Mofrad, 2008), where most models succeed in capturing at least some aspects of experimental data on NPCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior computational work, with multiple citations.

claim: It is critical to calibrate computational models and their parameters against well-controlled experiments.
source: The here observed sensitivity to parameter settings indicates that it is critical to calibrate computational models and their parameters against well-controlled experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the importance of experimental validation for computational models.

claim: Experimental data obtained on well-defined FG domain assemblies could serve as reference for calibration of computational models.
source: We propose that experimental data obtained on well-defined FG domain assemblies (such as those provided and used here), possibly complemented by structural data of isolated FG domains in solution (Yamada et al., 2010), could serve as reference for such calibration.
evidence: This is a proposal for how to improve computational modeling in the field.

claim: Given the observed insensitivity to chemical heterogeneity of the FG domains, one can estimate the level of detail that will need to be included for building an appropriate model of the NPC.
source: That said, given the observed insensitivity to chemical heterogeneity of the FG domains, one can estimate the level of detail that will need to be included for building an appropriate model and understanding of mechanisms of selective transport in the NPC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of future modeling efforts.

claim: It is essential to take into account the flexible nature and cohesion of FG domains, as well as the crowding of NTRs that bind to the FG domain assemblies.
source: The results presented here indicate that it is essential to take into account the flexible nature and cohesion of FG domains, as well as the crowding of NTRs that bind to the FG domain assemblies, but that heterogeneity at the scale of amino acids may only be of minor importance.
evidence: This is a conclusion about what features are important to include in models of the NPC.

claim: Heterogeneity at the scale of amino acids may only be of minor importance for modeling NPC transport.
source: The results presented here indicate that it is essential to take into account the flexible nature and cohesion of FG domains, as well as the crowding of NTRs that bind to the FG domain assemblies, but that heterogeneity at the scale of amino acids may only be of minor importance.
evidence: This is a conclusion about what features may not be critical to include in models of the NPC.

claim: The enrichment of NTRs into the FG domain phase is determined by generic physical effects and by the overall balance of a collection of low-affinity inter-FG-domain and NTR•FG domain interactions.
source: These results imply that the enrichment of NTRs into the FG domain phase is determined by generic physical effects – the flexible nature and spatial confinement of FG domains and the NTR size – and by the overall balance of a collection of low-affinity inter-FG-domain and NTR•FG domain interactions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental and computational results.

claim: Moderate changes in the overall balance of interactions cause remarkably large changes in the protein uptake by the FG domain assemblies.
source: Moreover, our computational data show that moderate changes in this overall balance cause remarkably large changes in the protein uptake by the FG domain assemblies, an observation that is fully consistent with the transport selectivity of the NPC.
evidence: This is a summary of the computational modeling results and their implications for NPC function.

claim: A similar approach may be viable to describe NPC transport selectivity in terms of generic polymer models.
source: Given the success of our model in replicating NTR binding behavior in a nanoscale mimic for the NPC, we therefore propose that a similar approach may be viable to describe NPC transport selectivity, i.e., in terms of generic polymer models, without necessarily taking into account the full amino acid sequences of FG domains and NTRs.
evidence: This is a proposal for future modeling approaches based on the success of the current work.

claim: Computational models need to be carefully calibrated to experimental data if they are to provide a meaningful contribution to the NPC field.
source: However, our results also show that computational models need to be carefully calibrated to experimental data – such as has been done in this work – if they are to provide a meaningful contribution to the NPC field, since small (~30% ) changes in interaction parameters can result in qualitatively different behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the importance of experimental validation for computational models.

claim: Small (~30%) changes in interaction parameters can result in qualitatively different behaviors.
source: since small (~30% ) changes in interaction parameters can result in qualitatively different behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary of the sensitivity to parameter changes observed in the computational modeling.
